item.title: The louder protectionism roars, the more precious China-EU dialogue becomes: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10 00:52:00
China EU Photo:VCG At a time when global challenges continue to emerge, the significance of China-EU relations has long extended beyond the bilateral sphere. By continuously deepening their economic ties and shared interests, China and the EU can not only unleash the innovative potential of their respective markets but also reinforce each other's development and contribute to global economic recovery. From Thursday to Friday, China and the EU held the second meeting of their bilateral trade and investment consultation mechanism in Beijing. The two sides engaged in pragmatic and productive discussions, reaching a 16-point consensus covering trade and investment balances, export controls, intellectual property rights and reform of the World Trade Organization (WTO). Against the backdrop of a sluggish global economic recovery and undercurrents of anti-globalization, this is a pragmatic step to properly handle bilateral differences and a crucial display of responsibility by China and the EU in injecting stability and certainty into the global economy amid turbulent times. A closer look at this list reveals its core value: anchored in rules-based governance and bridged by mutual trust, it demonstrates the political wisdom to manage differences and steer China-EU economic and trade relations toward greater stability and balance. The first item on the list states that both sides will continue to explore the possibility of reducing tariffs on certain products within the WTO framework. In the hybrid vehicle trade sector, which has attracted significant public attention, the two sides agreed to reach a mutual understanding in a manner consistent with WTO rules, providing a pathway to ease the previously deadlocked trade dispute. In the field of export controls, China expressed its willingness to continue facilitating export license approvals for rare earths and permanent magnets bound for the EU through a "green channel" mechanism. The two sides also included "advance notifications before items are added to control lists" in the consensus list. This arrangement improves the transparency in listing and delisting procedures, helping to reduce misjudgments and stabilize expectations. This list covers a significant portion of the current challenges and bottlenecks in economic and trade relations between China and the EU, and the consensus reached by both sides demonstrates that no matter how complex trade frictions may be, pragmatic solutions can always be found as long as both sides uphold the spirit of dialogue and adhere to equal-footed consultation. The convergence of interests is the inevitable outcome of economic globalization and more so a powerful engine driving common prosperity for China, the EU, and the world at large. In 2025, China-EU trade in goods exceeded $800 billion, with their combined economic output accounting for over one-third of the global total, bilateral trade volume making up nearly one-quarter of the world's total, and nearly half of bilateral trade consisting of intermediate goods. The long-standing pattern of "trade surpluses in China and profits in Europe" has made the two sides a community of shared interests, with each deeply intertwined with the other. This also demonstrates that as long as China and the EU work together, the synergies they generate will far outweigh the narrow calculations of a zero-sum game, creating vast new opportunities for industrial upgrading and improving the well-being of their peoples. Protectionism cannot enhance competitiveness, while decoupling and severing supply chains will only harm others without benefiting oneself. By continuously deepening their economic ties and shared interests, China and the EU can not only unleash the innovative potential of their respective markets but also reinforce each other's development and contribute to global economic recovery. As a major strategic force in the world, Europe should uphold its tradition of multilateralism and strategic autonomy, rather than allow itself to be swept up in the tide of protectionism and the excessive securitization of economic issues. At the moment, unilateralism is on the rise, with certain major powers frequently imposing sanctions in an attempt to weaponize economic and trade issues. Europe has a deep-rooted tradition of free trade and should not simply follow the crowd, much less turn security anxieties into trade barriers. As China has repeatedly and sincerely pointed out, the EU should remain committed to openness, cooperation and free trade, abide by WTO rules, not resort to protectionist tools at every turn, and, above all, refrain from politicizing and excessively securitizing economic and trade issues - so as to avoid pursuing misguided policies that will ultimately backfire on itself. China is not the root cause of the EU's problems, but a partner in addressing them. Faced with a complex external environment, Europe can only truly safeguard its fundamental interests amid changes unseen in a century by taking a long-term view of the economic and trade relations between China and the EU and adhering to equal-footed dialogue and consultation. Looking ahead to future arrangements for institutionalized consultations, China and the EU should overcome obstacles through sustained dialogue and work together to provide stability and certainty to the world. The two sides have agreed to hold the third regular meeting under the mechanism in March 2027 and maintain close communication in the meantime, including a ministerial-level video meeting in January 2027. Such institutionalized and regular arrangements provide an important safeguard for bridging differences and deepening cooperation. At a time when global challenges continue to emerge, the significance of China-EU relations has long extended beyond the bilateral sphere. In the face of an international landscape marked by intertwined turbulence and transformation, China and the EU should be partners that build mutual trust rather than systemic rivals, and promoters of cooperation rather than instigators of friction. We look forward to both China and the EU seizing this opportunity presented by the consultations to continue deepening cooperation based on equal dialogue and mutual benefit, translating more consensus into concrete actions, ensuring that the benefits of China-EU economic and trade cooperation continue to benefit the people of both sides, and injecting more warmth and confidence into a global economy fraught with uncertainty.

item.title: Chinese national killed in attack on construction site in Nigeria's Kebbi State: report
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10 00:33:00
Map of Kebbi State in Nigeria Photo: screenshot from a Channels Television report A Chinese national was killed along with two local security personnel in an attack on a construction site in Nigeria's Kebbi State on Thursday, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Friday, citing local police. According to Xinhua, the Kebbi State Police Command said in a statement on Friday that armed men entered the area from neighboring Sokoto State and attacked a construction site, killing a foreign national and two local security personnel. Police confirmed to Xinhua on Friday that the foreign national killed in the attack was a Chinese citizen, according to the report. Two other people were injured in the attack and taken to hospital for treatment, according to the police statement. Police also said they repelled another attack elsewhere in Kebbi State on Thursday, and security forces have been deployed to the affected areas to strengthen security, Xinhua reported. Global Times

item.title: Two Chinese porcelain objects reportedly damaged at British Museum, renewing calls for return of looted cultural relics
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10 00:13:00
Broken porcelain fragments are seen scattered across the bottom of a display case in Room 95 of the British Museum, while the mounting position marked "B629" appears empty. Photo: Screenshot from media reports The display shelf where the damaged objects had been exhibited in Room 95 of the British Museum, on October 10, 2026. Photo: Courtesy of Pan Jinyu Two Chinese porcelain objects dating to the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) Kangxi period at the British Museum were allegedly damaged on Sunday after a bowl fell from its display shelf. The museum reportedly said in response that neither the shelf nor its mounting showed signs of failure and that an investigation into the incident was continuing, according to Red Star News. According to the report, the two damaged objects, a bowl and a small box from the Sir Percival David collection, have now been handed over to the museum's conservation team for restoration. News of the incident first drew attention after photographs showing broken porcelain pieces at the bottom of a display case circulated on Chinese social media. Pan Jinyu, a self-described Chinese-language guide at the British Museum, told the Global Times on Friday that he returned to the gallery on October 7 and questioned museum staff after noticing that Room 95, where the objects had been displayed, was temporarily closed on October 4. "They seemed surprised that we had seen photos of it, but confirmed to me that porcelain had indeed been broken," he said. At the time, the label at the display position read "object removed for study," Pan said. By October 8, however, Pan said the labels had been changed, indicating that the two objects missing from their original display positions had been sent to "Destination: Conservation." "The labels appeared to have been updated after the incident attracted wider public attention," Pan said. Photos of the display case show a large number of Chinese porcelain objects arranged in close proximity on the shelves. Pan said the bowl had been displayed upside down on a support, apparently to show its base to visitors. From photos taken after it fell, he felt the mounting did not appear particularly secure and there was enough open space for the bowl to drop. He noted that such displays were relatively uncommon and that most other porcelain objects appeared to be securely positioned. The Global Times had contacted the British Museum for comment but had received no response as of press time. Notably, five days after the incident, the museum had yet to issue any public statement or explanation on the matter. Under many social media posts about the incident, netizens expressed frustration over what they saw as the British Museum's failure to properly safeguard and preserve valuable cultural relics, while renewed calls emerged for the many Chinese artifacts in British Museum to be returned home. "Still such a long road home," one netizen wrote. "Chinese cultural relics that were looted and scattered across the world embody the soul of Chinese culture. They must come home, and one day they will." Others put it more bluntly: "If you can't take proper care of them, give them back." Huo Zhengxin, a professor at the China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times that in 2002, major museums in Europe and the US, including the British Museum, cited their role in preserving, studying and displaying world cultural heritage as part of the rationale for retaining overseas collections. However, repeated thefts and damage at institutions including the British Museum in recent years have increasingly called that argument into question. For cultural relics taken overseas through illegal wartime plunder, colonial expansion or other improper means, the expert said that seeking their return is an inalienable sovereign right of the countries of origin and a necessary step toward restoring historical justice.

item.title: China vows necessary response if measures harm Chinese interests, after US meeting on 'excess capacity'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 23:18:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG China will make a necessary response if relevant economies use so-called "overcapacity" as a pretext to take measures that harm Chinese interests, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said on Friday. The remarks came in response to a question about an announcement issued by the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) on October 7 stating that it had convened a meeting of senior officials of 14 economies to begin work to address "structural excess capacity" and production in key manufacturing sectors, and the economies joined the US in signing a joint ministerial statement to address so-called "global excess capacity" and production in key manufacturing sectors. "We have noted the relevant developments," the MOFCOM spokesperson said, noting that China has repeatedly explained its views on the so-called "overcapacity" issue on different occasions and released a dedicated position paper in July this year. China has consistently maintained that capacity issues should be viewed in a comprehensive, objective and fair manner. Economic and trade issues should not be politicized out of concerns about one's own industrial competitiveness and market position, the spokesperson said. China remains committed to building a modern industrial system through openness and cooperation and supports the establishment of a fair and equitable international economic order, the spokesperson added. China calls on all relevant parties to uphold multilateralism, promote mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, respect market principles, and jointly safeguard an open and inclusive framework for global industrial and supply chain cooperation, the spokesperson said. Global Times

item.title: Chinese woman's A$50 thrift-store 'blind box' yields currencies from around the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 22:08:00
Coins from various countries are sorted after being taken out of the money jar. Photo: Xiaoxiang Morning Herald report A Chinese woman in Australia got more than she bargained for after spending A$50 ($34.70) on a secondhand money jar, only to discover dozens of currencies from around the world inside, turning the unusual thrift-store purchase into a small profit, Xiaoxiang Morning Herald reported. The woman, who goes by Stella online, told Xiaoxiang Morning Herald that she first came across the jar while casually browsing a charity thrift store on October 1, the first day of China's National Day holidays. She filmed it and posted the video online, where it quickly attracted attention. Curious viewers urged her to find out what was inside, so she returned the next day and bought it. The A$50 jar already showed a few visible banknotes and coins, including a 1-yuan Chinese banknote. Stella explained that the shop was a charity store where donated secondhand items are priced and resold, after some social media users wondered whether the seller was simply trying to make money from the mystery container. Once home, Stella spent more than two hours sorting through the haul. Among the finds were 150,000 Vietnamese dong, S$10, $5, 1 yuan and a variety of old coins. By the time she had separated the currencies into dozens of types, she said, it was already dark outside. A rough calculation put the collection's value at about 421.97 yuan ($63), leaving her more than 180 yuan ahead based on exchange rates. But Stella said she has no plans to cash in. Many of the coins are old and no longer in circulation, and she believes the original owner must have put considerable effort into collecting them. She plans to keep the collection as a souvenir. Global Times

item.title: From Northern Myanmar to the world, an anti-fraud dragnet is tightening
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 21:52:00
A sceenshot of The Demise of Telecom Fraud in Northern Myanmar. Source: CCTV Following its broadcast, the three-part documentary The Demise of Telecom Fraud in Northern Myanmar has caught widespread attention both in China and abroad. This reaction reflects a universal aversion to telecom fraud across the international community and a shared expectation for joint decisive action. Telecom fraud is a global scourge. According to a report by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, economic losses incurred by fraud in East and Southeast Asia, Australia, and other regions reached a staggering $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in 2025 alone - a figure that even exceeds the GDP of several countries. Perpetrators of telecom fraud have long dug in abroad, directing operations remotely. Meanwhile, funds move in seconds, digital trails are obfuscated through layers of disguise, and victims span multiple nations. Authorities shut down one fraud compound today only to see a new one spring up on another hill tomorrow, or arrest a few ringleaders here while a fresh batch of "agents" emerges elsewhere. This proves a stark reality: without cross-border cooperation - encompassing intelligence sharing, joint arrests, judicial collaboration, and repatriation - anti-fraud efforts are reduced to an endless game of "whack-a-mole," where stamping out one fire only sparks another elsewhere. How to join forces to sever the tentacles of telecom fraud has become a question that is imperative for the international community to answer. The solution demonstrated by China in this battle is to advance international cooperation through concrete action. As revealed in the third episode of the documentary Weaving the Sky Net, Chinese and Myanmar police, leveraging long-standing law enforcement and security cooperation mechanisms, carried out their first joint enforcement operation in Muse town in Myanmar, apprehending 807 telecom fraud suspects in a single sweep and eradicating the final, most stubborn "nail" that had long resisted the special crackdown. Meanwhile, the ministerial-level coordination mechanism established by China, Myanmar, and Thailand in early 2025 launched joint purges against gambling and fraud syndicates in Myanmar's Myawaddy town, carrying out 10 consecutive joint repatriation operations that led to the total demolition of more than 630 buildings in the infamous KK Park. For China, tightening this anti-fraud dragnet is both an essential requirement for safeguarding the property security of its own people and a concrete practice of fulfilling its responsibilities as a major country to build a community with a shared future for humanity. At the law enforcement level, China has repeatedly launched joint crackdown operations with Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and other countries. At the institutional level, China and its neighboring countries have successively established trilateral coordination mechanisms among China, Myanmar, and Thailand, as well as the Lancang-Mekong law enforcement and security cooperation mechanism. Furthermore, China has helped neighboring nations build law enforcement capacity through material assistance and technical support. Not long ago, the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud was established in Lianyungang, East China's Jiangsu Province, where representatives from 46 founding countries, 34 observer countries, the United Nations, Interpol, and other bodies issued a joint declaration. This marks a pivotal shift in global anti-fraud efforts - coordinated and advanced by China - from a fragmented "sweeping snow from one's own doorstep" approach to "jointly weaving an integrated global network." Combating telecom fraud is no overnight task, and in the fight against fraud, there are no bystanders. Facing telecom fraud that constantly shifts and mutates, only through broader consensus, more pragmatic measures, and a tighter network can the chain of evil be broken and the peace and well-being of millions of households safeguarded.

item.title: GT on the spot: How do Yangshan Port immigration officers pair AI screening with sniffer dogs to keep the world's busiest gateway moving?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 21:42:00
A section of Shanghai Yangshan Deep Water Port Photo: VCG An overseas cargo vessel slowly approached the port. In the bridge, the captain could not yet make out the coastline with the naked eye, but on a giant screen at the Command Center of the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station, about 35 nautical miles away, the ship's bright signal had already been firmly detected. The vessel berthed. The gangway was lowered. Crew members disembarked one by one, while their luggage passed through X-ray scanners, their faces were matched, and their travel documents were verified - all in a matter of seconds. At the same time, live footage was fed back to the command center in real time. On both sides of the quay crane, smart sensors automatically captured the body language, clothing and facial features of embarking and disembarking crew, with the data instantly cross-referenced against Border Inspection Clearance Channel and port security gates. This is Shanghai Yangshan Deep Water Port, the world's largest man-made deep-water port built on an island. As a key component of Shanghai Port - which has ranked first in the world in container throughput for 16 consecutive years - Yangshan Deep Water Port handled more than 28 million TEUs (twenty-foot equivalent units) in 2025, accounting for as much as 52 percent of Shanghai Port's total throughput. At this world-class hub that operates around the clock, how can security and efficiency be achieved at the same time? The Global Times reporter recently visited the Phase IV automated terminal of the Yangshan Deep Water Port, and the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station, to experience firsthand a smart security line woven by "AI algorithms" and the "nose of police dogs." The Command Center of the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station Photo: Huang Lanlan/GT 'All-seeing eyes' Yangshan Deep Water Port is bigger than many people imagine. More than 20,000 container trucks enter and leave the port area every day, and an average of about 450 authorized boarding personnel conduct work operations daily. Like a set of precision gears spinning at high speed, the terminal has become a vast, tightly coordinated system - one that the local immigration authorities say can no longer be effectively managed by the old-style inspection model that relied on face-to-face, on-site checks. The transformation began with an intelligent sensing system. At the Command Center of the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station, immigration officer Li Daming demonstrated how the system works. Far out at sea, in the anchorage area, a photoelectric radar covers a radius of 30 nautical miles, bringing every vessel that enters the zone under surveillance. Closer in, detection checkpoints have been set up along the main shipping channel, through which all inbound vessels must pass. "This system has been upgraded over the past few years. It's like installing a pair of 'all-seeing eyes' on the sea," Li told the Global Times. But technology is not always enough. Some deep-sea cargo vessels have complex structures, with tightly packed containers and numerous hidden gaps and interlayers - blind spots that may escape both machines and human eyes. That is why local immigration officers also use another "tool." On an early fall afternoon at local immigration inspection station, the Global Times reporter saw suitcases being lined up on the ground. Hidden inside one of them was a small packet of cannabis. A police dog named "Manman," led by handler Zhang Xiaobin, sniffed its way slowly past the luggage, tail gently swaying. It eventually stopped beside the suitcase concealing the drugs and barked. Four-and-a-half-year-old Manman is a Labrador trained to detect narcotics and has already taken part in multiple real-world operations. In September 2023, the Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station established its police dog unit, which now has seven dogs trained for narcotics detection, explosives detection, patrol and security work, as well as special search-and-rescue tasks. In August 2025, the police dog unit helped uncover contraband during an inspection on a ship's deck. Immigration officers train police dogs to detect narcotics at Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station on August 26, 2026 Photo: Huang Lanlan/GT Better service Yangshan Deep Water Port's bustle is not confined to cargo. In the first half of 2026, more than 4,700 international vessels berthed at the port. Every day, crew members from around the world enter China through this gateway. "The route network here spans more than 200 countries and regions, and the crew come from places such as Russia, the Philippines, India, Ukraine, Sweden and Germany," said immigration officer Wang Jing. To cope with the port's high-density, high-volume operations, Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station has further streamlined clearance procedures to better serve those involved. For those who board ships to visit relatives working as crew members, the process has also become far simpler. "In the past, they had to come to the immigration inspection station in person to apply for a permit. Now, they can do it online," Wang said. Similarly, overseas crew members who need to go ashore only have to obtain a temporary entry permit for seafarers. They can submit their applications online in advance, and on-site immigration officers only need to verify their identity documents against the person present. "As long as it's within the permitted time frame, crew members can easily go shopping or sightseeing in downtown Shanghai," Wang told the Global Times. Data showed that in 2025, Yangshan Immigration Inspection Station processed 10,500 outbound vessel clearances, 259,000 passenger movements and 15,000 crew changeovers. From AI-powered "all-seeing eyes" and drug-sniffing police dogs, to almost contactless clearance, the safety and efficiency of Yangshan Deep Water Port continue to rise. "Every container at this world's largest port is tied to the national port security," Li told the Global Times. "There is no end to port development, and neither will our safeguarding efforts ever stop."

item.title: How China achieved its photovoltaic turnaround
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 21:21:00
Solar rooftop photovoltaic power generation facilities are seen on a building in Qingdao, East China's Shandong Province, on June 23, 2026. Photo: VCG By the end of July, China's installed capacity of solar panels reached 1.286 billion kilowatts in China, surpassing that of coal power for the first time to become the nation's largest power source by installed capacity. In China, photovoltaic (PV) power has shifted from a "satellite-exclusive luxury" to a power source cheaper than coal. This remarkable turnaround offers deep insights into industrial growth and the fundamental laws of energy transition. The essence of this turnaround lies in locking the market and the factories into a single closed-loop system, driving that ecosystem toward systematic synergy and high-efficiency operation. To get this virtuous cycle spinning, the first step was a vigorous push to expand the domestic market. China has been leveraging policy coordination to anchor and open up the domestic market. Measures included shifting subsidies entirely to actual power generation output with 20-year guaranteed terms. This not only plugged loopholes prone to subsidy fraud but also provided stable, long-term revenue streams, turning solar farms into bankable assets that financial institutions were willing to lend to. The foresight of this policy lay not merely in daring to invest when solar costs remained high, but in building a mechanism that forced costs downward rather than simply throwing subsidies at enterprises to keep them afloat. Truly effective industrial policy does not replace the market; rather, it allows market forces to play out fully over long cycles. Once the market opened, cost reduction shifted to continuous technological innovation, driven by compounding, chain-reaction improvements rather than single breakthroughs. Innovations like diamond wire saws slashed silicon wafer costs and established mono-crystalline wafers as the mainstream choice, a trajectory mirrored by PERC solar cell technology. These technologies were not originally invented in China, but why were their industrialization fates ultimately rewritten in Chinese workshops? The reason lies in China's comprehensive, all-inclusive industrial supply chains and intense market competition. The moment a new manufacturing process is successfully verified and run at a single company, domestic equipment suppliers immediately step up with iterative upgrades, and industry peers race to expand production capacity, achieving widespread adoption across the entire sector within a few years. Today, China's PV industry R&D strength has entered the global vanguard. Besides, technology dictates the content of learning, while scale determines its speed. China accounts for over 80 percent of manufacturing output across all segments of the solar supply chain, meaning the vast majority of global PV industrial experience has been accumulated in China. The true weight of China's scaled industrial capacity lies in the fact that its expanding output can, by and large, find genuine, real-world demand to absorb it, be it at home or abroad. When supply can be manufactured and demand can absorb it, costs can slide steadily down the "learning curve." Of course, the industry faces pressing real-world challenges in integration and absorption. On the power grid side, midday surges in solar generation coupled with insufficient support during evening peak hours mean that energy storage deployment and market mechanisms urgently need strengthening. On the industrial side, harmonizing industrial policy with effective measures to curb cutthroat price competition and realigning the supply side with genuine market demand are vital tasks for the period ahead. From a "luxury item on satellites" to a ubiquitous fixture on deserts, rooftops, and fish ponds, solar power has journeyed for over seven decades since the invention of the silicon solar cell. The answer behind China's solar turnaround is hardly a secret: policy guided the market back home, an integrated supply chain system translated innovation into scaled manufacturing capacity, and an ultra-large market and application ecosystem further refined that capacity into seasoned industrial expertise. Chinese enterprises had paid the "tuition fee," and today, the dividends and hard-earned lessons of cost reduction are shared with the world. For the world, the profound significance of China's PV turnaround lies in shattering conventional mindsets: energy security does not have to be entirely tethered to underground reserves and maritime trade routes; at least a portion of it can be forged right inside a workshop. The author is a research fellow at the Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Risk Perception and Sustainable Governance in Energy Transition. Fu Hongdi also contributed to this article. opinion@globaltimes.com.cn

item.title: Tourism spending up 4.3% during National Day holidays: ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 21:15:00
Passengers enter the Beijing South Railway Station during the National Day holidays. Photo: VCG China's recent seven-day National Day holidays set a new benchmark for domestic tourism, with some 826 million trips made during the period and domestic tourism spending exceeding 738 billion yuan ($110.11 billion), according to latest data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism (MCT) on Friday. On a comparable and averaged daily basis, the number of trips increased 6.3 percent and tourism spending was up 4.3 percent year-on-year. Analysts said that this year's National Day holidays saw robust supply and demand, as well as coordinated growth across multiple sectors. From cultural and tourism experiences and brick-and-mortar commercial districts to big-ticket consumption, all areas saw strong momentum, reflecting China's consumption vitality, they said. According to the MCT, tourism market supply continued to diversify during the holiday. Red tourism was highly popular, with 40 percent of tourists visiting revolutionary venues, watching national flag-raising ceremonies, attending patriotic performances, and taking part in other related activities. Rural tourism continued to gain momentum, with autumn sightseeing, intangible cultural heritage experiences, farming and picking, nighttime rural tours, bonfire markets, and rice-field concerts widely welcomed, the ministry said. The performance market also boomed, with 180 large-scale performances held nationwide, including 125 concerts and 55 music festivals. Various localities across the country held a variety of cultural and tourism activities to attract tourists and distributed more than 310 million yuan in consumption coupons as a support measure. National-level nighttime culture and tourism consumption clusters recorded a total nighttime footfall of 107 million, up 5.6 percent year-on-year. The inbound tourism market was also active. Nationwide, 2.983 million inbound tourist visits were recorded, representing a year-on-year increase of 19 percent from 2024 and 6.5 percent from 2025. Zhang Yiwu, a professor with Peking University, told the Global Times on Friday that the longer holiday period this year allowed many people to go on long-haul tours and people's choices of destination were also more diversified than before. Unconventional tourist sites and especially county-level attractions have become a highlight this year, Zhang noted. According to data sent to the Global Times by domestic platform Tongcheng Travel, Urumqi, capital of Northwest China's Xinjiang, ranked top among domestic long-haul destinations. With tourism supply seeing a marked improvement in quality in recent years, immersive travel experiences and service-related consumption have become the trending choice this year, Zhang said, noting that shows, sports events, concerts and cinema add more facets to the colorful holiday life of the people. Also on Friday, China's railway operator posted robust transportation data for the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays. China's railways recorded more than 302 million passenger trips from September 23 to October 8 during the 16-day railway travel rush for the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays, up 24.6 percent year-on-year, China State Railway Group Co said on Friday. During the period, 192 million tons of goods were shipped, up 5 percent year-on-year. On October 1, 25.2 million passenger trips were handled, setting a single-day record.
